title: Identifying Effective Indicators for In-Season Potato Nitrogen Status Diagnosis Using Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches
content: Effective nutrient management is essential for potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) production, offering both economic and environmental benefits due to the crop’s high nitrogen (N) demand and typically low N use efficiency. Best management practices recommend petiole analysis for guiding in-season N fertilizer application. Other N condition indicators (NCIs) may also reflect potato N status, but practical constraints limit their use. Proximal and remote sensing technologies may help overcome those constraints. The objectives were 1) to systematically compare NCIs’ agronomic efficacy relative to yield, and 2) derive stage-specific optimum values for the most effective NCIs by yield simulation and evaluate them against published sufficiency ranges. Data from nine site-years of plot-scale N rate experiments conducted in Minnesota, USA between 2015 and 2024 were consolidated for analysis. The effectiveness of 10 NCIs (i.e., petiole nitrate-N concentration, vine/plant N concentration, aboveground/whole plant biomass, vine/plant N uptake, three types of N nutrition index (NNI)) plus SPAD meter readings were systematically evaluated with reference to relative total yield. Linear correlation, partial least squares regression, and random forest regression were employed in the analysis workflow, both with and without considering the additional effects of different potato cultivars and water stress factors. Petiole nitrate-N concentration was particularly informative during early growth stages, whereas the biomass-based NCIs remained consistently informative across all growth stages. The SPAD meter reading was a strong non-destructive indicator, sometimes outperforming the destructively measured indicators. The simulated petiole nitrate-N concentration optima broadly approximated the lower bounds of the published sufficiency ranges, with 88.2% agreement in the resulting N status classifications (Cohen’s kappa = 0.73). More research is needed to extend this comparison to additional cultivars, environments, and sensing platforms, and to translate the resulting ranking of NCIs into practical in-season N status diagnosis in potatoes.
